transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-09-09 15:00 UTC
- Duration: 48 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Derek Walsh (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Asha Rao (TideCrest Head of ML), Ben Morales (TideCrest Platform Eng), Claire Kim (TideCrest FinOps), Jordan Lee (TideCrest SRE)

Summary:
Quick console walkthrough focused on per-route usage analytics and cost decomposition. Customer wants clarity on how Redwood attributes cost to routes, how to map model variants and batching to cost buckets, and how to run a low-effort bench for expected query mix. Decision criteria: predictable unit cost per route, exportable reports for FinOps, and ability to pin model versions for production.

Topics:
- Route-level telemetry and tagging
- Token/unit cost attribution across model variants and quantization profiles
- Exporting cost reports and integration with internal billing
- Bench plan: sample prompts, expected QPS, latency targets
- Security notes (data retention, SSO)

Action items (captured in notes): see metadata

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account, um we've got Derek and Priya from solutions engineering here, how's it going at TideCrest?
[00:06] Asha: Hey Maya, hi all, we're good, excited to see the console side, Claire's here for the cost questions.
[00:10] Ben: Hey, yeah quick note, we've been.. we've been running some internal endpoints and spend has crept up, so curious about per-route attribution.
[00:16] Maya: Totally, that's the goal today. We'll walk through the usage dashboard, then the per-route breakdown, and the cost decomposition — and leave time for a short bench plan.
[00:24] Derek: Quick callout before i jump in, we'll use the sample TideCrest routes that Claire shared earlier, and i'll show how to map them to cost buckets in the console.
[00:31] Claire: Sounds good. also, small ask — can you show how we export the CSV for our internal FinOps tool?
[00:36] Priya: Yep we have export and S3 push, i'll show both.

[01:02] Derek: Ok sharing screen (link to deck: https://rwd.company/decks/tidecrest-console-demo). Starting on the top-level "Usage" page — this is where you get an at-a-glance of tokens, requests, and latency per day. You'll notice the timeline at the top, and down below are the routes.
[01:20] Asha: I see. Are routes automatically created from API keys, or do we have to tag them?
[01:27] Derek: Both options. By default routes are inferred from the API key and path, but for clean billing we recommend explicit route tagging — that gives you deterministic attribution across environments.
[01:36] Ben: If i tag a route as "chat-product-recs" will it show up across the org?
[01:40] Derek: It will show up in your org with role-based visibility — admins see everything, you can limit dashboards with RBAC.
[01:47] Jordan: Quick sec — how does batch time factor into latency on the console? our SRE is worried about tail latency if batching is aggressive.
[01:54] Priya: Good Q. The console shows both observed latency and effective per-request latency after batching. You can filter by model or route. We also surface distribution percentiles (p50/p95/p99). For tail-sensitive routes we recommend smaller batch thresholds or dedicate Dedicated capacity with lower batching windows.
[02:12] Claire: When you say "per-request latency after batching" is that an average token-level amortized metric or wall-clock per API call?
[02:18] Derek: It's amortized across the batch; the console shows both the amortized token cost and the wall-clock latency so you can reason about trade-offs.
[02:25] Asha: Can you show the per-route cost decomposition? that's the main thing we need.
[02:30] Derek: Jumping there now. Under "Routes > Cost" you'll see a stacked bar with route-level spend split by model variant, batch savings, and cache hits.
[02:39] Maya: Note: sometimes the transcription (sorry) — the console header says "route economics" but you might see it as "route-eco" in older tenants, there's some naming drift in the UI if you've used earlier betas.
[02:50] Ben: Haha, good to know.
[03:00] [03:00] Derek: Here's a sample route, "product-recs-chat" — you can expand to see token counts, model used (gptx-8b-q4a), quantization profile, and estimated GPU time. That last bit is backfilled from the runtime.
[03:18] Claire: Where does the model variant cost number come from? is it list price or runtime-measured compute?
[03:24] Derek: It's a blended metric: runtime-measured GPU seconds times our per-second cost model, plus a token-processing surcharge that captures misc infra overhead. We surface both the raw compute cost and the final billed line for transparency.
[03:36] Asha: Does Redwood apply any smoothing if a route spikes? we don't want weird month-to-month jumps in reported unit cost.
[03:43] Priya: We do smoothing for visualization but billing exports are raw by-interval. In the console you can choose a 7-day or 30-day rolling average for unit cost.
[03:53] Ben: Show the CSV export please.
[03:56] Derek: Sure. Export button — you can choose columns: route, model, tokens_in, tokens_out, requests, avg_latency_ms, billed_cost_usd, compute_seconds, quant_profile. Then choose S3 target or download.
[04:10] Claire: Great, we want an S3 push to our acct for daily reconciliation.
[04:14] Maya: We can enable S3 pushes and provide an IAM role for push. I'll include the config snippet.
[04:20] Jordan: Asha, from infra side we need to know if KV cache savings are visible too.
[04:26] Derek: Yes — KV cache hit rate is a separate column; the cost view shows "cache-saved-tokens" and estimated cost avoided. The cache is counted per model family and route.
[04:36] Asha: How does pinning a model version affect routing and cost?
[04:39] Priya: If you pin, requests to that route are routed to that model variant; pinning ensures consistent behavior for quality testing. The console shows a "pinned" badge and the cost view will attribute spend to the pinned variant. If pinned variant is unavailable we can fallback to a compatible variant per your rollout policy.
[04:55] Ben: Walk me through an example: route A used gptx-8b-q4a and then we roll to gptx-8b-int8 which is cheaper — how do we compare?
[05:03] Derek: The console's compare mode lets you select two time windows or two model variants and shows delta in tokens, compute_seconds, and cost. We'll also run simulated cost with your sample traffic to project savings if you switch to int8.
[05:18] Claire: Do you show quantization tradeoffs? like estimated quality regression metrics?
[05:22] Maya: We can surface evaluation set diffs if you upload a prompt set. Redwood Optimize ties in here — it can run a lightweight eval and flag regressions against thresholds. We'll show a quick example.
[05:34] Derek: Opening the Optimize panel — here's a historical eval we ran for a customer; it shows BLEU/EM-like metrics and human-pass rates. For TideCrest we can ingest your NLU classification prompts and run a small sweep.
[05:47] Asha: That would be helpful.
[05:49] [06:00] Derek: Quick pause — there's some minor lag on my screen share, bear with me.
[06:15] Derek: Back. Now, on the cost decomposition we also surface "batch savings" — that's an estimated USD saved due to batching and KV cache. For example, this route saved 23% of cost from batching last month.
[06:30] Ben: Is batching saving shown as an absolute dollar reduction or percentage?
[06:33] Derek: Both. The stacked bar has absolute USD by component and we show % savings as a tooltip.
[06:40] Jordan: In practice, how do we forecast cost if our QPS doubles?
[06:44] Priya: There's a forecast panel where you can change QPS, mix of models, and it simulates spend across your selected routes and timeframe. We also export a scenario CSV.
[06:55] Claire: For procurement, we need to see committed Reserved capacity vs burst charges.
[06:59] Maya: On the billing tab we show committed coverage percentage and any overage. If you buy Dedicated, we can allocate capacity to route groups for predictable throughput and lower per-token compute charge.
[07:12] Asha: Security quick Q: data retention, do you store prompts in Redwood?
[07:16] Derek: By default we retain logs for 30 days; for enterprise we can turn off prompt retention, or route logs to your VPC. We support SSO/SAML and KMS integrations — we'll attach SOC2 docs after the call.
[07:29] Ben: any limit on S3 export size or retention?
[07:32] Priya: No hard limits; exports can be daily or hourly. We'll work with your infra on the bucket lifecycle.
[07:38] Asha: ok can we see an example of a route-level anomaly alert? we had weird spikes last month.
[07:44] Derek: Sure. Alerts -> create -> select route -> threshold on requests or cost per minute -> notify via webhooks or Slack. Here's an example policy that alerted on >150% increase in requests vs rolling 7d.
[07:58] Claire: Do alerts include cost delta when they fire? we want automated tickets when cost goes above threshold.
[08:03] Derek: Yep, payload includes current cost and projected 24h trend; you can map to your ticketing system.
[08:10] Maya: Want to switch to the bench plan quick? Derek will outline steps to run a 1k-request bench with TideCrest prompts.
[08:17] Derek: Bench plan: 1) you provide 200 representative prompts (Claire to confirm sample), 2) we run 1k requests with your QPS profile (we typically do bursts then steady), 3) we capture per-route token counts, latency, and compute_seconds, 4) export CSV and a short explainer.
[08:34] Claire: I can export sample prompts by EOD tomorrow.
[08:37] Asha: Target SLO is 300ms p95 for our customer-facing routes. Can Redwood hit that on Hosted or do we need Dedicated?
[08:45] Derek: For 300ms p95 on complex models, Hosted can hit it for low-moderate QPS; for sustained higher QPS Dedicated with pinned instances is recommended. The bench will help you see where Hosted suffices.
[08:58] Ben: If we go Dedicated, how's cost modeled? flat monthly + usage?
[09:03] Maya: Dedicated is a reserved capacity contract — monthly commit for base pricing and metered overage at a lower incremental rate. We'll share a pricing matrix.
[09:12] Jordan: Any gotchas on private deploys? we might need air-gapped eventually.
[09:16] Priya: On-prem is supported but has longer lead times. VPC private deploy is typical for regulated data and supports your KMS.
[09:25] Asha: Ok thanks. A few follow-ups — can you also show how to map routes to internal chargeback tags? we want to tie cost back to product teams.
[09:35] Derek: Yes that's the tagging feature — you can attach arbitrary key:value tags to routes and then roll up cost by tag. We'll demo that in your tenant during the POC.
[09:45] Claire: One more finance Q — do you include third-party cloud egress or infra license fees in the billed cost?
[09:52] Maya: We show the Redwood portion; if you're on a marketplace or there are pass-through infra fees we can include them in a consolidated export if you provide the numbers; alternatively, for Dedicated we can incorporate partners' costs into the committed pricing.
[10:05] Asha: Awesome.
[10:10] Derek: Wrapping up the demo, quick recap of what we'll send: pricing + playbook, bench plan + timeline, SOC2 and SAML docs, and a hands-on POC scoping doc.
[10:21] Ben: Sounds good.
[10:23] Claire: we'll aim to share sample prompts and monthly spend export by 2026-09-12.
[10:29] Maya: Great. I'll email the calendar holds for POC scoping and include a sample IAM role for S3 exports.
[10:36] Jordan: One last note — when you run the bench, can you simulate our mixed traffic (50% chat, 30% embedding, 20% rerank)?
[10:44] Derek: Yep we'll do proportional mixes and show per-route metrics.
[10:48] Asha: Thanks everyone, that was helpful.
[10:50] Maya: Thank you all, we'll follow up with materials.
[10:53] [End of recording]

Notes on transcription quality: medium — a few product names and acronyms mis-heard ("K-V cash" for KV cache in one excerpt), occasional speaker label swaps, and some cut words where bandwidth hiccuped.
